note: Establish a compact backbone targeting the valuable C5 stream first, with moderate stages/reflux and lower pressures.
notebook: PLAN: Start with high-value C5 recovery while cutting lights and C6+ away; inspect purities/costs, then add only profitable branches (C3/C4 blends and heavy products). Step 1: test root C4/C5 split, C5/C6 split, and isopentane/n-pentane separation.

note: Sharpen the two backbone cuts and split the light overhead into sellable C3 and C4 blends, removing the premature heavy branch.
notebook:
PLAN: Build sharp C4/C5 and C5/C6 splits, sell C3, C4 and C5 blends first; then add C6-paraffin and heavy-product branches only if margins justify them. Step 1: raise root/B separation enough for blend purity and add a C3/C4 split.
Initial 50/2/2 root leaked heavily: only 42% n-butane overhead and C5 contaminated both outlets. Costs are substantial (~$70-155M per modest column), so target 95% blends rather than 99% pure products and avoid redundant polishing. Current test uses 60 stages and R=B=4 at the two difficult backbone cuts, with a smaller 45/3/3 C3/C4 column.

note: Switch to the highest-value C6 paraffin blend: recover C5 and lighter overhead, then cut C6 paraffins from naphthenes and heavies.
notebook:
PLAN: First monetize the high-value C6 paraffin blend with a C5/C6 root split and a C6-paraffin/C6-naphthene bottoms split. Then add C5 and light-blend recovery, and finally assess heavy products. Step 1: two-column C6 backbone.
The prior C4/C5-oriented root at 60/4/4/dp.3 sent about half the C5 overhead and yielded no sellable stream. C6 paraffins are worth roughly $1.1B/yr as a blend, much more than the light blends. Root now targets all C5 and lighter overhead; B targets 2,2-DMB through n-hexane overhead, leaving methylcyclopentane and heavier in BB. Lower column pressure should improve relative volatility. Avoid the former T column until the valuable blend meets 95%.

note: Sharpen the C5/C6 root cut and give the difficult n-hexane/methylcyclopentane split enough stages and reflux to sell the C6 paraffin blend.
notebook:
PLAN: First monetize the high-value C6 paraffin blend with a C5/C6 root split and a C6-paraffin/C6-naphthene bottoms split. Then add C5 and light-blend recovery, and finally assess heavy products. Step 1: sharpen the two-column C6 backbone.
The first backbones left too much C5 in B and C6 naphthenes in BT. C6 paraffins are worth roughly $1.05B/yr as an 85%-discount blend, so justify high reflux here. Root boil-up must lift essentially all isopentane/n-pentane but little 2,2-DMB. B must split n-hexane from methylcyclopentane, a close cut, so raise it to 80 stages and R=7. Lower pressure improves volatility. Avoid spending on light columns until BT sells.

note: Add a C4/C5 splitter to the clean root overhead so its concentrated isopentane/n-pentane bottoms can sell as the C5 blend.
notebook:
PLAN: Monetize the C6 paraffin blend first, then recover the C5 blend from root tops, followed by light blends and selected heavy products. Step 2: add a C4/C5 splitter on T while retaining the profitable C6 backbone.
The current root makes a sharp C5/C6 cut and B gives a qualifying C6-paraffin stream worth $941.9M/yr. Root T contains about 695 mol/s C5 with only C4 and lighter contaminants, so a single butane/isopentane split should create a C5 blend worth roughly $600M/yr. Use moderate stages/reflux to control cost; defer further light splits until this sale is established.

note: Make the C4/C5 split much sharper so the large C5 bottoms stream actually reaches blend specification.
notebook:
PLAN: Monetize the C6 paraffin blend first, then recover the C5 blend from root tops, followed by light blends and selected heavy products. Step 2: sharply split C4 from C5 on T while retaining the profitable C6 backbone.
The root/B backbone sells the C6 paraffin blend for $941.9M/yr and alone scored 0.728. T at 55/4/3.5 leaves TB only 79% C5, so its added cost is not yet justified. C4/C5 volatility is favorable; increase T to 80 stages with reflux and boil-up 8 to push n-butane overhead and isopentane downward. Target >95% C5 in TB (~$619M/yr), then split TT into C3 and C4 blends if economics support it.

note: Adopt the proven high-reward backbone and add three moderate heavy-end splitters to recover heptane, octane, and nonane from the currently worthless BB stream.
notebook:
PLAN: Start from the island-best C5/C6/n-butane backbone, then monetize the clean C7+ heavy cut with a compact three-column train; optimize light ends only afterward.
R262 shows that moderate T boil-up (55/5/7), not excessive stages/reflux, achieves 95% C5 cheaply; TT at 45/4/5 recovers 96% n-butane. Copy it. Its BB still contains C6s plus heptane, octane and nonane. A BB split between cyclohexane and heptane should isolate C7+, followed by heptane/octane and octane/nonane splitters. These wide boiling gaps should allow moderate 45-50 stage columns and roughly $795M/yr base product value (more at 99% purity). Leave the C6-rich BBT stream unsold for now; later consider C3 recovery and sharper root-B separation.

note: Remove the unproductive C6 naphthene splitters and instead recover heptane, octane, and nonane from the clean C7+ bottoms with two wide-gap splits.
notebook:
PLAN: Use the proven C5/C6/n-butane backbone; monetize C7+ with heptane/octane and octane/nonane splitters, then improve light ends and root economics.
The first heavy branch was misplaced: BB sends substantial C6/n naphthenes overhead, and further BBT splitters cannot make a 95% product, so their ~$95M/yr cost is wasted. BBB is a clean 440 mol/s mixture of heptane (33%), octane (53%), and nonane (14%), ideal for two sequential wide-gap splits. Remove BBT and split BBB at heptane/octane, then its bottoms at octane/nonane. Moderate 50-stage, 3.5-reflux columns should recover about $795M/yr of base C7+ value. If successful, tune purity versus column cost; do not pursue the failed C6 naphthene branch.

note: Adopt the cheaper, higher-recovery C6 splitter and sharpen both clean C7+ separations, especially heptane overhead and nonane bottoms.
notebook:
PLAN: Use the proven C5/C6/n-butane backbone; monetize C7+ with sharpened heptane/octane and octane/nonane splitters, then optimize light ends and root economics.
The inexpensive B=70/6/5 configuration improves C6 recovery and cuts cost versus 80/7. The heavy BBB stream is a clean C7+ mixture, but 50-stage/3.5-reflux operation leaves heptane tops at only 62%; sharply increase both ratios to reject octane overhead. BBBB already makes premium octane but loses 35 mol/s octane to nonane bottoms, so increase boil-up to recover it and purify nonane. Keep the unproductive BBT branch removed. If heavy purity responds, tune costs afterward.

PLAN: Adopt the 2.269 backbone, then make the clean C7+ branch sell heptane and nonane without excessive duty; afterward optimize light ends and column costs.
R402 shows BBB=50/5/3 gives 78% heptane with only 33 mol/s octane overhead, unlike high boil-up. Increase rectification (60 stages, reflux 8) and reduce boil-up to 2 to target 95% heptane. R402's BBBB has premium octane but 53% octane bottoms; raise boil-up to 8 and reflux to 5 to recover octane overhead and approach nonane purity. Preserve the proven C5/C6 backbone.

note: Adopt the 2.603 plant and strongly increase stripping in the octane/nonane splitter to recover the remaining nonane product.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the 2.603 heavy train, recover nonane with a much higher BBBB boil-up, then optimize light ends and dominant column costs.
R453 gives premium heptane with BBB=60/8/3 and 98% octane with BBBB=60/8/7. Its nonane bottoms still contain 100 mol/s octane, so a materially larger stripping ratio is needed to sell nonane. Try BBBB reboil 15; preserve all proven backbone settings.

note: Add a compact polisher to the nonane-rich BBBB bottoms; the wide octane/nonane volatility gap should recover both stranded products cheaply.
notebook:
PLAN: Finish the heavy-end recovery with a small octane/nonane polisher, then reduce the dominant backbone costs and test selective premium upgrades.
Current BBBBB is only 106 mol/s but contains about 62 nonane and 44 octane. A separate wide-boiling-gap split should recover roughly $175M/yr of extra product for a modest column cost. R501 used 45/4/6 on a larger, less favourable feed and obtained 100% octane and 90% nonane; this richer feed should clear both specifications.

note: Reduce the C4/C5 splitter size and duties; both current products have useful purity margin, so this is a direct cost-saving test.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the saleable cuts while reducing the dominant backbone costs; test the C4/C5 splitter first, then the C6 and root columns, and only then consider extra recovery.
Best is 2.897. Heavy train is effective; avoid double effect (R552 failed thermally and economically). Current T costs $168.6M/yr and both outlets have comfortable purity: TTB is 96% n-butane and TB is a clean C5 blend. Test 45 stages, reflux 4, boil-up 6 to seek substantial savings without losing either product. Root changes are expensive in solves because all descendants must be resimulated.

note: Adopt the highest-reward proven island plant, preserving its profitable naphthene recovery and improved octane/nonane train.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt the proven R649 naphthene/heavy train as the new baseline, then use the remaining solves on profitable polishing or backbone cost reductions without disturbing its clean cuts.
R649 gives 3.219 versus my 2.940: the naphthene branch adds $155M/yr net of its two columns, while BBBB at reflux 4 and the strong BBBBB polisher improve octane/nonane recovery. Preserve T=45/4/6, BBBB=60/4/15 and BBBBB=60/8/6. Likely next tests: improve BBTB recovery/purity or trim dominant root/B costs only with cautious settings.

note: Trim the two dominant backbone columns; their clean cuts and saleable products may tolerate substantially lower size and duties.
notebook:
PLAN: Preserve the R649 product train and test cautious reductions in the two dominant backbone columns; if product quality holds, continue trimming, otherwise revert and polish recovery.
R649 baseline 3.219: root and B cost $607.7M/yr, over half total cost. Both outlet cuts are clean and all products have margin, so test root 55/4/5 and B 60/5/4 first. R695 showed stronger BBTB hurts, and R694 showed TTT splitting gives no saleable product. Preserve T=45/4/6, BBBB=60/4/15, BBBBB=60/8/6.

note: Adopt the proven 3.443 plant and increase stripping in the small nonane polisher; its 28 mol/s overhead is already 77% nonane, so a modest purity gain could create another sale.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R743 as the new baseline (3.443), then use remaining solves on small terminal-column improvements; retain the best valid result if a test is weaker.
R743 adds BBTBB=60/6/6/0.2, recovering 62 mol/s premium heptane for only $23M/yr and reaching 3.443. R740's stronger 60/8/10 version is worse, so avoid it. The remaining small opportunity is BBBBB: its 28 mol/s overhead is 77% nonane and unsold, while 41 mol/s pure nonane bottoms already sells. Increasing boil-up from 6 to 10 may push the overhead over 95% nonane without materially losing bottoms recovery. Preserve the backbone: trimming root/B destroyed the C6 blend and octane sales.

note: Adopt the proven 3.544 plant and trim both small terminal columns; the heptane finisher is already proven at 45/5/5, and the cyclohexane finisher has useful purity margin.
notebook:
PLAN: Adopt R791's 3.544 plant, then use the last solves only on low-risk terminal-column cost trims; preserve the best valid design.
R791 adds BBTBBT=60/6/6/0.2 and sells 27 mol/s premium cyclohexane, adding $55M/yr revenue for $10.8M/yr cost. R789 proves BBTBB can be trimmed to 45/5/5 with pure heptane bottoms and lower cost. Test both terminal columns at 45/5/5. Nonane overhead remains unsellable at higher stripping; do not revisit it. Root/B trims destroyed major sales.

note: Adopt R838's island-best finisher and trim only BBTBB to the already-proven 45/5/5 setting, saving cost without changing its downstream feed.
notebook:
PLAN: Copy island-best R838 and use one final solve on its proven-safe BBTBB trim; then stop and preserve the best valid result.
R838's 60/8/10 BBTBBT finisher makes 30 mol/s premium cyclohexane and earns 3.550. R789/current plant prove BBTBB at 45/5/5 still yields pure heptane bottoms while saving about $3.8M/yr. Its BBTBBT feed is unchanged, so no other re-solve is needed. Nonane overhead and root/B changes are unproductive; do not revisit.

note: Adopt the 3.573 plant and make one final intermediate stripping adjustment to the binary finisher, targeting saleable heptane bottoms without losing the premium cyclohexane overhead.
notebook:
PLAN: Copy island-best R886 and spend the final solve between its proven 70/10/12 finisher (pure cyclohexane, 92% heptane bottoms) and the over-stripped 60/8/15 case; 70/10/13 targets both products saleable.
R886 earns 3.573 through higher nonane recovery. Its tiny binary finisher needs only slightly more stripping: at boil-up 12 the bottoms are 92% heptane, while boil-up 15 makes heptane pure but sacrifices cyclohexane purity. A modest increase to 13 should preserve the premium overhead while pushing bottoms over 95%. All other columns are copied unchanged and previously solved.
